solution:
| Basis of difference | Respiration | Combustion |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | A biochemical process that occurs within living cells | A physico-chemical process that does not need a living cell |
| Steps | Oxidation occurs in a **series of slow, step-wise reactions** | Oxidation occurs **in one step**, rapidly |
| Enzymes | Every step is **controlled by enzymes** | No enzymes are involved |
| Release of energy | Energy is released gradually and much of it is **trapped as ATP** | All the energy is released at once; **most of it is given out as heat** (and light) |
| Temperature | Occurs at the ordinary temperature of the cell | Needs a high temperature |
| Intermediates | Intermediates are formed; the carbon skeletons are used as **precursors for biosynthesis** | No useful intermediates are formed |
| End products | \(\text{CO}_2\), \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) and energy stored in ATP | \(\text{CO}_2\), \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\), heat and light |
groundedIn: §12.0; §12.1 — respiration is oxidation within cells in slow step-wise reactions controlled by enzymes, energy trapped as ATP, carbon skeleton used as precursors for biosynthesis; complete combustion of glucose yields energy most of which is given out as heat, glucose oxidised in several small steps rather than one; BEYOND CHAPTER: combustion is non-enzymatic, needs no living cell, needs a high temperature and gives out light, while respiration runs at ordinary cell temperature

solution:
| Basis of difference | Glycolysis | Krebs' cycle |
|---|---|---|
| Site | **Cytoplasm** of the cell | **Matrix of the mitochondria** |
| Occurrence | Present in **all living organisms**, aerobic and anaerobic; the only process of respiration in anaerobes | Occurs only in **aerobic respiration**; requires \(\text{O}_2\) supply |
| Starting and end products | Glucose (6C) is partially oxidised to **two molecules of pyruvic acid** (3C) | Acetyl CoA (2C) is completely oxidised; oxaloacetic acid is regenerated and \(\text{CO}_2\) is released |
| Nature of pathway | A **linear** chain of ten reactions | A **cyclic** pathway (tricarboxylic acid cycle) |
| \(\text{CO}_2\) release | No \(\text{CO}_2\) is released | \(\text{CO}_2\) is released at two decarboxylation steps in each turn |
| ATP (per glucose) | 4 ATP formed, 2 ATP used: **net gain of 2 ATP** | **2 ATP** (formed via GTP by substrate level phosphorylation) |
| Reduced coenzymes (per glucose) | **2** \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) | **6** \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) and **2** \(\text{FADH}_2\) |
| Worked out by | Gustav Embden, Otto Meyerhof and J. Parnas (**EMP pathway**) | **Hans Krebs** |
groundedIn: §12.2; Fig. 12.1; §12.4.1; Fig. 12.3; §12.3; §12.5 — glycolysis in cytoplasm of all living organisms, EMP pathway by Embden, Meyerhof and Parnas, glucose to two pyruvic acid by ten reactions, ATP used at two steps and formed at two steps per triose, net gain of two ATP; TCA cycle in mitochondrial matrix, requires O2, two decarboxylations, three NADH and one FADH2 per turn, GTP gives ATP, Hans Krebs

solution:
| Basis of difference | Aerobic respiration | Fermentation |
|---|---|---|
| Oxygen | Takes place in the **presence of \(\text{O}_2\)** | Takes place under **anaerobic conditions** |
| Breakdown of glucose | **Complete** oxidation of glucose to \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) | Only **partial** (incomplete) breakdown of glucose |
| End products | \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) | **Ethanol and \(\text{CO}_2\)** (yeast) or **lactic acid** (some bacteria, muscles) |
| Energy yield | A large amount of energy; a net gain of up to **38 ATP** per glucose | Less than seven per cent of the energy in glucose is released; a net gain of only **2 ATP** per glucose |
| Oxidation of NADH | \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) is oxidised to \(\text{NAD}^+\) **very vigorously** | \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) is oxidised to \(\text{NAD}^+\) **rather slowly** |
| Site (eukaryotes) | Glycolysis in the cytoplasm; the remaining steps in the **mitochondria** | Occurs entirely in the **cytoplasm** |
| Occurrence | Most common in higher organisms | Many prokaryotes and unicellular eukaryotes; muscle cells when \(\text{O}_2\) is inadequate |
groundedIn: §12.3; §12.4; §12.5 — fermentation under anaerobic conditions in many prokaryotes and unicellular eukaryotes, yeast gives CO2 and ethanol, bacteria and exercising muscles give lactic acid, less than seven per cent of energy released; aerobic respiration complete oxidation in the presence of oxygen, steps within mitochondria, most common in higher organisms; comparison: partial vs complete breakdown, net two ATP vs many more, net gain of 38 ATP, NADH oxidised slowly vs vigorously; BEYOND CHAPTER: fermentation occurs entirely in the cytoplasm

stem: What are respiratory substrates? Name the most common respiratory substrate.
solution:
**Respiratory substrates** are the compounds that are oxidised during respiration to release energy. Usually **carbohydrates** are oxidised, but **proteins, fats** and even **organic acids** can be used as respiratory substrates in some plants under certain conditions.

The most common respiratory substrate is **glucose**; it is the favoured substrate for respiration, and other carbohydrates are usually first converted into glucose before they are respired.
groundedIn: §12.0; §12.6 — compounds oxidised during respiration are respiratory substrates; usually carbohydrates, but proteins, fats and organic acids in some plants; glucose is the favoured substrate and all carbohydrates are usually first converted into glucose

stem: Give the schematic representation of glycolysis?
solution:
**Glycolysis (EMP pathway)** takes place in the **cytoplasm**. One molecule of glucose (6C) is partially oxidised to **two molecules of pyruvic acid** (3C) through a chain of **ten enzyme-controlled reactions**:

1. Glucose (6C) \(\xrightarrow{\text{ATP} \rightarrow \text{ADP}}\) **Glucose-6-phosphate** (6C) (enzyme hexokinase)
2. Glucose-6-phosphate \(\rightarrow\) **Fructose-6-phosphate** (6C) (isomerisation)
3. Fructose-6-phosphate \(\xrightarrow{\text{ATP} \rightarrow \text{ADP}}\) **Fructose 1, 6-bisphosphate** (6C)
4. Fructose 1, 6-bisphosphate \(\rightarrow\) **3-phosphoglyceraldehyde (PGAL)** (3C) + **dihydroxyacetone phosphate** (3C)
5. Dihydroxyacetone phosphate \(\rightleftharpoons\) PGAL (the two triose phosphates are interconvertible)
6. PGAL + Pi \(\xrightarrow{\text{NAD}^+ \rightarrow \text{NADH} + \text{H}^+}\) **1, 3-bisphosphoglyceric acid (BPGA)** (3C), \(\times 2\)
7. BPGA \(\xrightarrow{\text{ADP} \rightarrow \text{ATP}}\) **3-phosphoglyceric acid (PGA)** (3C), \(\times 2\)
8. PGA \(\rightarrow\) **2-phosphoglycerate**, \(\times 2\)
9. 2-phosphoglycerate \(\xrightarrow{-\,\text{H}_2\text{O}}\) **phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP)**, \(\times 2\)
10. PEP \(\xrightarrow{\text{ADP} \rightarrow \text{ATP}}\) **pyruvic acid** (3C), \(\times 2\)

**Balance per glucose:** 2 ATP used (steps 1 and 3), 4 ATP formed (steps 7 and 10), so a **net gain of 2 ATP**, and **2** \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) formed (step 6).
groundedIn: §12.2; Fig. 12.1; §12.5 — glycolysis in the cytoplasm, ten reactions under different enzymes; hexokinase phosphorylates glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, isomerised to fructose-6-phosphate; ATP utilised at glucose to G6P and F6P to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate; split into DHAP and PGAL; PGAL to BPGA forms NADH + H+; BPGA to PGA and PEP to pyruvic acid each form ATP; 2-phosphoglycerate loses H2O to PEP; net gain of two ATP per glucose

stem: What are the main steps in aerobic respiration? Where does it take place?
solution:
**Aerobic respiration** is the complete oxidation of organic substances in the presence of oxygen, releasing \(\text{CO}_2\), water and a large amount of energy. In eukaryotes it takes place in the **mitochondria** (after glycolysis in the cytoplasm).

**Main steps:**

1. **Glycolysis** (cytoplasm): glucose is broken down to two molecules of pyruvic acid, which are transported into the mitochondria.
2. **Oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate** (mitochondrial matrix), catalysed by **pyruvic dehydrogenase**:
\(\text{Pyruvic acid} + \text{CoA} + \text{NAD}^+ \xrightarrow[\text{Pyruvate dehydrogenase}]{\text{Mg}^{2+}} \text{Acetyl CoA} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\)
3. **Tricarboxylic acid (Krebs') cycle** (mitochondrial matrix): acetyl CoA is completely oxidised by the stepwise removal of all its hydrogen atoms; \(\text{CO}_2\) is released and \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) and \(\text{FADH}_2\) are formed.
4. **Electron transport system and oxidative phosphorylation** (**inner mitochondrial membrane**): electrons from \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) and \(\text{FADH}_2\) are passed on to molecular \(\text{O}_2\), forming water, with simultaneous synthesis of ATP.

Thus the first process (removal of hydrogen) takes place in the **matrix** and the second (passing electrons to \(\text{O}_2\) with ATP synthesis) on the **inner membrane** of the mitochondria.
groundedIn: §12.3; §12.4; §12.4.1; §12.4.2 — aerobic respiration complete oxidation in presence of oxygen, steps take place within the mitochondria; pyruvate transported into mitochondria; oxidative decarboxylation by pyruvic dehydrogenase with NAD+ and CoA; TCA cycle; crucial events are stepwise removal of hydrogen in the matrix and passing electrons to O2 with ATP synthesis on the inner membrane; ETS in inner mitochondrial membrane

stem: Give the schematic representation of an overall view of Krebs' cycle.
solution:
The **Krebs' cycle (tricarboxylic acid / citric acid cycle)** runs in the **mitochondrial matrix**.

**Link step:** Pyruvate (3C) + CoA + \(\text{NAD}^+ \rightarrow\) **Acetyl CoA** (2C) + \(\text{CO}_2\) + \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\)

**The cycle:**

1. Acetyl CoA (2C) + **oxaloacetic acid (OAA)** (4C) + \(\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow\) **citric acid** (6C) + CoA (enzyme citrate synthase)
2. Citrate \(\rightarrow\) isocitrate (isomerisation)
3. Isocitrate \(\rightarrow\) **α-ketoglutaric acid** (5C) + \(\text{CO}_2\); \(\text{NAD}^+ \rightarrow \text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\)
4. α-ketoglutaric acid \(\rightarrow\) **succinyl-CoA** (4C) + \(\text{CO}_2\); \(\text{NAD}^+ \rightarrow \text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\)
5. Succinyl-CoA \(\rightarrow\) **succinic acid** (4C); \(\text{GDP} \rightarrow \text{GTP}\) (substrate level phosphorylation), and GTP gives ATP from ADP
6. Succinic acid \(\rightarrow\) **malic acid** (4C); \(\text{FAD} \rightarrow \text{FADH}_2\)
7. Malic acid \(\rightarrow\) **oxaloacetic acid** (4C); \(\text{NAD}^+ \rightarrow \text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\). OAA is regenerated and the cycle continues.

**Summary equation:**
\(\text{Pyruvic acid} + 4\text{NAD}^+ + \text{FAD} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{ADP} + \text{Pi} \xrightarrow{\text{Mitochondrial Matrix}} 3\text{CO}_2 + 4\text{NADH} + 4\text{H}^+ + \text{FADH}_2 + \text{ATP}\)

Each turn of the cycle gives 2 \(\text{CO}_2\), 3 \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\), 1 \(\text{FADH}_2\) and 1 ATP; one glucose gives two turns.
groundedIn: §12.4; §12.4.1; Fig. 12.3 — pyruvate to acetyl CoA with CO2 and NADH; acetyl group condenses with OAA and water to citric acid by citrate synthase; citrate isomerised to isocitrate; two successive decarboxylations to alpha-ketoglutaric acid and succinyl-CoA; succinyl-CoA to succinic acid forms GTP then ATP; three NAD+ and one FAD+ reduction points; OAA regenerated; summary equation in the mitochondrial matrix

solution:
The **electron transport system (ETS)** is the metabolic pathway through which electrons pass from one carrier to another. It is present in the **inner mitochondrial membrane** and releases the energy stored in \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) and \(\text{FADH}_2\), the electrons finally passing to \(\text{O}_2\) to form \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\).

1. **Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase)** oxidises the NADH produced in the citric acid cycle; its electrons are transferred to **ubiquinone** in the inner membrane.
2. **Complex II** passes reducing equivalents from \(\text{FADH}_2\) (formed during oxidation of succinate) to ubiquinone.
3. Reduced ubiquinone (**ubiquinol**) is oxidised by the **cytochrome bc\(_1\) complex (complex III)**, which transfers the electrons to **cytochrome c**.
4. **Cytochrome c**, a small protein on the outer surface of the inner membrane, acts as a **mobile carrier** between complex III and complex IV.
5. **Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase)**, containing cytochromes a and a\(_3\) and two copper centres, passes the electrons to \(\text{O}_2\), the **final hydrogen acceptor**, forming water.
6. The electron flow is coupled to **ATP synthase (complex V)**, which makes ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate: one NADH gives **3 ATP** and one \(\text{FADH}_2\) gives **2 ATP**.
groundedIn: §12.4.2; Fig. 12.4 — ETS is the pathway through which electrons pass from one carrier to another in the inner mitochondrial membrane; complex I NADH dehydrogenase to ubiquinone; FADH2 via complex II; ubiquinol oxidised by cytochrome bc1 complex III to cytochrome c, a mobile carrier between III and IV; complex IV cytochrome c oxidase with cytochromes a and a3 and two copper centres; coupled to ATP synthase complex V; NADH gives 3 ATP, FADH2 gives 2; oxygen the final hydrogen acceptor

| Enzymes of the final steps | Ten glycolytic enzymes, e.g. hexokinase | **Pyruvic acid decarboxylase** and **alcohol dehydrogenase** (alcoholic), **lactate dehydrogenase** (lactic acid) |

stem: What are the assumptions made during the calculation of net gain of ATP?
solution:
The net gain of **38 ATP** per glucose molecule in aerobic respiration is calculated on these assumptions:

1. There is a **sequential, orderly pathway** functioning, with one substrate forming the next, and with **glycolysis, TCA cycle and ETS** following one after another.
2. The **NADH synthesised in glycolysis is transferred into the mitochondria** and undergoes oxidative phosphorylation.
3. **None of the intermediates** in the pathway are utilised to synthesise any other compound.
4. **Only glucose is being respired**; no other alternative substrates enter the pathway at any of the intermediary stages.

These assumptions are not really valid in a living system, so the calculation remains a theoretical exercise.
groundedIn: §12.5 — calculations made on assumptions: sequential orderly pathway with glycolysis, TCA and ETS one after another; glycolytic NADH transferred into mitochondria; no intermediates used to synthesise other compounds; only glucose respired; assumptions not valid in a living system; net gain of 38 ATP

stem: Discuss "The respiratory pathway is an amphibolic pathway."
solution:
A pathway involved in both **catabolism** (breaking down) and **anabolism** (synthesis) is called **amphibolic**. The respiratory pathway is amphibolic for these reasons:

1. Traditionally respiration was considered **catabolic**, since it breaks down substrates to release energy.
2. Different substrates enter the pathway at different points: **fats** are broken into glycerol and fatty acids; **fatty acids** are degraded to **acetyl CoA**; **glycerol** enters after conversion to **PGAL**; **proteins** are degraded by proteases and the amino acids (after **deamination**) enter as pyruvate, acetyl CoA or within the Krebs' cycle.
3. The **same compounds are withdrawn** from the pathway for synthesis of these substrates. For example, when the organism needs to synthesise **fatty acids**, acetyl CoA is withdrawn from the respiratory pathway.
4. Similarly, during the breakdown and synthesis of **proteins**, respiratory intermediates form the link.

Since the respiratory pathway is involved in **both anabolism and catabolism**, it is better considered an **amphibolic pathway** rather than a catabolic one.
groundedIn: §12.6; Fig. 12.6 — respiration traditionally considered catabolic; fats to glycerol and fatty acids, fatty acids to acetyl CoA, glycerol to PGAL, proteins by proteases and amino acids after deamination enter as pyruvate, acetyl CoA or in Krebs' cycle; acetyl CoA withdrawn for fatty acid synthesis; respiratory intermediates link protein breakdown and synthesis; involved in both anabolism and catabolism so amphibolic

stem: Define RQ. What is its value for fats?
solution:
**Respiratory quotient (RQ)**, or respiratory ratio, is the ratio of the volume of \(\text{CO}_2\) evolved to the volume of \(\text{O}_2\) consumed in respiration:

\(\text{RQ} = \dfrac{\text{volume of CO}_2 \text{ evolved}}{\text{volume of O}_2 \text{ consumed}}\)

For **fats**, the RQ is **less than 1**. For example, for tripalmitin:

\(2(\text{C}_{51}\text{H}_{98}\text{O}_6) + 145\,\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 102\,\text{CO}_2 + 98\,\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{energy}\)

\(\text{RQ} = \dfrac{102\,\text{CO}_2}{145\,\text{O}_2} = \mathbf{0.7}\)
groundedIn: §12.7 — RQ is the ratio of the volume of CO2 evolved to the volume of O2 consumed in respiration, also called respiratory ratio; when fats are used RQ is less than 1; tripalmitin equation gives RQ = 102 CO2 / 145 O2 = 0.7

solution:
**Oxidative phosphorylation** is the synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate using the energy of **oxidation-reduction** released as electrons from \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) and \(\text{FADH}_2\) pass through the **electron transport system** to \(\text{O}_2\) in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

1. The energy of oxidation-reduction (not light energy, as in photophosphorylation) is used to produce the **proton gradient** required for phosphorylation.
2. ATP is made by **ATP synthase (complex V)**: its **\(\text{F}_0\)** part forms the channel through which protons cross the inner membrane, and its **\(\text{F}_1\)** headpiece contains the site for synthesis of ATP.
3. For each ATP produced, **4 \(\text{H}^+\)** pass through \(\text{F}_0\) from the intermembrane space to the matrix.
4. Oxidation of one NADH gives **3 ATP** and of one \(\text{FADH}_2\) gives **2 ATP**.
5. **Oxygen** acts as the **final hydrogen acceptor** and is reduced to water.
groundedIn: §12.4.2; Fig. 12.5 — energy of oxidation-reduction rather than light energy produces the proton gradient, hence oxidative phosphorylation; ATP synthase complex V with F1 headpiece site of ATP synthesis and F0 proton channel; 4H+ per ATP from intermembrane space to matrix; NADH gives 3 ATP, FADH2 gives 2; oxygen the final hydrogen acceptor

stem: What is the significance of step-wise release of energy in respiration?
solution:
The **step-wise release of energy** allows the cell to **trap the energy as ATP** instead of losing it as heat.

1. Complete combustion of glucose in one step would release energy, **most of which is given out as heat**, which the cell cannot use.
2. When glucose is oxidised in **several small steps**, some steps release energy just large enough to be **coupled to ATP synthesis**.
3. Each step is **controlled by enzymes**, so the release of energy is slow and regulated.
4. The energy trapped in **ATP**, the energy currency of the cell, is used whenever and wherever it is needed for energy-requiring processes.
5. The step-wise breakdown forms **intermediates**; their carbon skeletons are used as **precursors for the biosynthesis** of other molecules in the cell.
groundedIn: §12.0; §12.1; §12.6 — energy released in a series of slow step-wise reactions controlled by enzymes and trapped as ATP, the energy currency; carbon skeleton used as precursors for biosynthesis; complete combustion gives energy mostly as heat; glucose oxidised in several small steps so energy released can be coupled to ATP synthesis; intermediates withdrawn for synthesis
